summary: Defines default integrity and confidentiality security contexts for Bundle Protocol Security. They can be used to test that BPSec implementations work together, and to provide basic protection when no other security contexts are defined or required for a network.

eli5.summary: These are the starter locks to try out the security system and to use when no better locks are chosen.

what are integrity scope flags in bpsec
subtitle: The two ready-made security recipes, HMAC integrity and AES-GCM encryption, for securing Bundle Protocol traffic.

tldr.problem: Bundle Protocol Security (BPSec) defines security blocks but needs concrete security contexts, so that implementations can interoperate and networks without their own contexts still get basic protection.
tldr.mechanism: BIB-HMAC-SHA2 puts a keyed hash over the protected data in a Block Integrity Block, and BCB-AES-GCM encrypts a block's data with AES in Galois/Counter Mode and adds an authentication tag, both using symmetric keys and CBOR encoding.
tldr.outcome: The contexts serve both as an interoperability test baseline and as default protection when no other contexts are defined or required. The appendix has worked examples usable in test suites.

today: RFC 9173 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2022 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is meant to be used together with BPSec (RFC 9172) and the Bundle Protocol (RFC 9171).

sections.title: Why Default Security Contexts
sections.content:
The Bundle Protocol Security specification (RFC 9172) provides integrity and confidentiality for bundles in networks that use the Bundle Protocol (RFC 9171). BPSec defines extension blocks that carry security information produced under some security context.

This RFC defines two such contexts, one for integrity and one for confidentiality, for populating Block Integrity Blocks (BIBs) and Block Confidentiality Blocks (BCBs). They are meant for testing interoperability and for basic security when no other context is defined or required. The information they generate MUST be encoded with CBOR (RFC 8949).

Both contexts use symmetric-key cryptography. The stated reason is that symmetric keys fit places where an asymmetric-key infrastructure such as a public key infrastructure might be impractical, and key management in delay-tolerant networks is hard because round trips may not be reliable or timely.
sections.eli5: Two programs that want to talk safely need to agree on which locks to use. This RFC picks two standard locks so everyone starts with the same ones.

sections.title: BIB-HMAC-SHA2: Integrity
sections.content:
The BIB-HMAC-SHA2 context produces a keyed-hash message authentication code over a plaintext called the Integrity-Protected Plaintext (IPPT). It combines SHA-2 with HMAC (RFC 2104). The HMAC output MUST equal the SHA-2 hash size: 256, 384 or 512 bits.

The IPPT always contains the security target's block-type-specific data and the integrity scope flags. Optional extras are controlled by three flag bits: bit 0 (0x0001) includes the primary block, bit 1 (0x0002) includes the target header (block type, number and processing flags), and bit 2 (0x0004) includes the security header of the BIB itself. Including the primary block ties a block to one bundle, so a block and its BIB copied into another bundle would fail verification.

There are three optional parameters. The SHA variant is 5, 6 or 7 for HMAC 256/256, 384/384 or 512/512, defaulting to 6. The wrapped key holds the HMAC key encrypted with AES key wrap (RFC 3394), and without it verifiers find the key from local policy. The integrity scope flags are a 16-bit value defaulting to 7. The single result is the expected HMAC, a byte string.

HMAC keys MUST be symmetric with a length equal to the HMAC output. Implementations SHOULD compare tags in constant time, because side-channel timing attacks could otherwise help an attacker guess a valid tag.
sections.eli5: It makes a fingerprint of a message using a secret key. If anyone changes the message, the fingerprint no longer matches, and the receiver knows.

sections.title: BCB-AES-GCM: Confidentiality
sections.content:
The BCB-AES-GCM context replaces a target block's data with ciphertext from AES in Galois/Counter Mode. GCM was chosen because symmetric keys are smaller, it avoids needing a public key infrastructure, the ciphertext is the same size as the plaintext (so length fields need no change), and it provides the authenticated encryption BPSec requires. Two variants exist, A128GCM (value 1) and A256GCM (value 3), with 3 as the default.

Parameters are the initialization vector (IV), AES variant, wrapped key and AAD scope flags. The IV MUST be 8 to 16 bytes, and 12 bytes SHOULD be used unless policy requires otherwise. An IV MUST NOT be reused with the same key. The AAD scope flags work like the integrity scope flags, with the same three bits and default 7, and select what extra data gets authenticated. The one result is a 128-bit authentication tag, which MAY be stored in the BCB or appended to the ciphertext in the target block.

GCM has strict rules. Reusing an IV and key pair makes the implementation open to forgery attacks, which the RFC calls catastrophic. The RFC recommends fewer than 2^64 AES blocks per key and requires no more than 2^32 invocations of the authenticated encryption function per key. Implementations SHOULD limit unsuccessful verification attempts per key. GCM has no replay protection of its own, and delay-tolerant networks see more replay attacks, so implementors SHOULD try to detect replays.
sections.eli5: It scrambles the message so only people with the key can read it, and it adds a small stamp that shows if anyone fiddled with the scrambled message.

sections.title: Building and Checking the Protected Data
sections.content:
Both contexts rely on canonicalization: turning each piece into one exact byte form so sender and receiver feed identical input to the algorithm. Forms are produced as described in RFC 9172. The IPPT or AAD starts with the CBOR encoding of the scope flags (for example 0x07 when all three bits are set), then appends, in order, the primary block, the target header fields and the security block header fields when the matching flags are set, and for the integrity context finally the target's data.

Before generating a hash or encrypting, any CRC on the target block MUST be removed and its CRC type set to "no CRC is present." When the service is removed at a security acceptor that is not the destination, and no other service protects the block, a CRC MUST be added back.

For decryption, the key comes from the wrapped key parameter if present and otherwise from local policy. If the ciphertext fails to authenticate or parameters are missing, decryption is treated as failed and handled per local policy. A failed HMAC verification is likewise treated as a failure under local policy.
sections.eli5: Before locking or checking a note, both sides write it out in exactly the same neat way, so the same note always gives the same answer.

sections.title: Key Handling and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Key management is not defined here. BPSec assumes it is handled as part of network management, so nodes must set up shared key-encrypting keys (KEKs) out of band, decide when keys are exhausted or invalid, and decide which keys go with which security blocks. Failing to do this can compromise the keys and lose the security services.

Keys SHOULD be protected in storage and in transit. A compromised key means operations using it should not be treated as providing integrity or confidentiality. The same key MUST NOT be used for different algorithms, and a KEK MUST NOT wrap keys for different security contexts, so one KEK must not serve both BIB-HMAC-SHA2 and BCB-AES-GCM.

Bundle fragmentation also causes trouble. A security block and its target in different fragments cannot be processed until reassembly, and a block bound to the primary block cannot be verified in a fragment, since fragments have different primary blocks. The RFC suggests encapsulating the bundle first and then fragmenting the encapsulating bundle.
sections.eli5: The locks are only as good as the key handling. If a key leaks, the lock is useless, and a key for one kind of lock should never be used to open another kind.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and Test Examples
sections.content:
IANA assigned two security context identifiers in the registry from RFC 9172: value 1 for BIB-HMAC-SHA2 and value 2 for BCB-AES-GCM. Two new registries, for the integrity scope flags and the AAD scope flags, use the Specification Required policy with 16-bit values. Designated experts must check that new flags clearly state how they change the IPPT or AAD, and that they do not alter required behavior.

Appendix A is informative. It walks through four examples, simple integrity, simple confidentiality with key wrap, security blocks from multiple sources and security blocks with full scope, showing the CBOR encodings. The RFC says they can inform unit test and interoperability test suites, though they do not cover every parameter combination.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives each lock a number in a public list, and includes worked examples so people can check their own work against known answers.
